name: Iron Cross
label: Dischord
lede: Sab Grey moved into the Dischord House in 1981 with an Oi! haircut and started what Wikipedia counts as the first band in the US to take on both the skinhead look and the sound. Three songs on Flex Your Head, one EP and one song called "Crucified" later, the band was being picketed in print while the song went off to live in other people's hands.

eras.title: A Baltimore skin at the Dischord House
eras.text: Sab Grey came down to DC shows with the Baltimore punk crowd, and by the time he moved to town in 1981 he'd traded punk for an Oi! look. He lived at the Dischord House, found two younger players who'd already been in bands together, and started a group that was rowdier than the neighborhood's reputation.

years.h: Sab Grey takes a room at the Dischord House
years.p: A regular at D.C. shows by way of Baltimore, Grey becomes one of the many residents of the house in Arlington. "I lived at Dischord house, it's not like I lived in a tree," he told Vice in 2012.

years.cap: Sab Grey singing and Wendell Blow on bass at the Wilson Center, Washington DC, spring 1982
years.h: Grey finds a drummer with spiked hair and two skinheads
years.p: Grey teams with drummer [[Dante Ferrando|98b1e2a2-3868-47f0-b905-35637b5a902f]], guitarist [[Mark Haggerty|235b9917-3f4c-4670-ade3-d94f8e45a044]] and bassist John Falls. Ferrando is the only one with spiked punk hair; the rest are skinheads.
years.xp:
Dischord dates the start to early 1981; Wikipedia says 1980, when Ferrando met Grey, and the band's 2012 EP is titled Est. 1980. Wikipedia says Grey suggested the name.

Grey has said the early DC scene was far rowdier than its clean-living reputation: drinking, smoking and fighting.

years.cap: Sab Grey and Wendell Blow at the Wilson Center, Washington DC, spring 1982
years.h: John Falls walks after American University; three bassists follow
years.p: Falls leaves after an early show at American University. [[Cynthia Connolly|bd50eae3-e00b-48c4-9b7d-4a7a41150ce2]] and [[Chris Haskett|963aeedd-f71e-4b09-8e65-76fc9ddde611]] pass through before [[Wendel Blow|6604fe5c-1a16-4689-861e-8658255eaf09]] arrives from the just-ended [[SOA|e54cb250-3502-4c32-9482-70488bd9a8cb]].

eras.title: Flex Your Head, then the exits
eras.text: Dischord's Flex Your Head put Iron Cross in front of a national audience next to Minor Threat and SOA. Almost as fast, the crowd the band drew started to worry its own members, and the original lineup came apart.

years.h: Three songs on Flex Your Head, between Minor Threat and SOA
years.p: "War Games", "New Breed" and "Live for Now" introduce Iron Cross to listeners well outside the East Coast on Dischord No. 7.
years.xp:
The three songs were recorded at C.A.B. Studios rather than Inner Ear.

Wikipedia says the compilation took the band past the audience it had on the East Coast.

years.p: The EP carries the band's signature song. TKO has since reissued it, and Dischord distributes the TKO version.
years.xp: The song is about being blamed for things because of how you look. Wikipedia reads it that way; its later life as an anthem is in 1987 below.

years.cap: Lyle Preslar, John Dunn, Wendell Blow and Sab Grey with Amy Pickering and Monica Richards, Georgetown, Washington DC, spring 1982
years.h: Wendel Blow is first to go; John Dunn and Paul Cleary take the bass
years.p: Per Dischord, Blow is the first member to leave. Original D.C. skin John Dunn steps in, and later Paul Cleary.

years.cap: Dante Ferrando outside the 9:30 Club, Washington DC, spring 1982
years.h: Ferrando and Haggerty walk out and start Gray Matter
years.p: Uneasy that Iron Cross's image was reflecting its violent supporters more than its members, the two quit to form [[Gray Matter|c9065214-ba09-4c2c-b341-35713b702264]]. From here Sab Grey fronts a revolving lineup.
years.xp: Wikipedia has Ferrando going on to open DC's Black Cat nightclub.

years.h: Hated and Proud arrives on Skinflint Records
years.p: The band's second EP, with Paul Cleary on bass after John Dunn.

eras.title: Branded the enemy
eras.text: The name and the shaved heads drew accusations of fascism, which the band always denied. By 1985 Grey was the last original member and he stopped arguing.

years.big: "They just decided one day that we were the enemy and that was it."
years.h: Maximum Rocknroll brands Iron Cross fascists
years.p: Critics, led by Tim Yohannan's Maximum Rocknroll, cast the band as fascists. Sab Grey told Vice in 2012 that they never checked the facts; the band said it hated Nazis.
years.xp:
Grey's complaint is that nobody asked. "Don't just make up crap and then spout it without getting the facts," he told Vice. Wikipedia notes he felt the intolerance ran toward him for being white.

Both things were true at once: the band denied any fascist politics, and the name and look made it a magnet for people who had them. It's what drove Ferrando and Haggerty out.

years.cap: Sab Grey at the Wilson Center, Washington DC, spring 1982
years.h: Grey calls it, and in 1986 moves to England
years.p: With the fascism charges still trailing the band, Sab Grey ends Iron Cross. A year later he's in England playing rockabilly and country.
years.xp: After the split Grey "hung around for about a year not really doing much," he told Vice, before leaving for England.

eras.title: "Crucified" leaves home
eras.text: The song Iron Cross is remembered for became everybody's anthem. Agnostic Front made it a New York hardcore staple, and it spread to skinheads of every politics, including the ones the band said it hated.

years.cap: Agnostic Front's Liberty and Justice For... (1987) carries their studio version of "Crucified"
years.h: Agnostic Front record "Crucified" for Liberty and Justice For...
years.p: The New York band had played the song live since the mid-'80s. The studio version follows on Liberty and Justice For... and again on Something's Gotta Give.
years.xp:
Wikipedia describes the song as an anthem for communist, anarchist and apolitical skinheads and for white power sympathizers alike, with live crowds adding "skinhead army!" chants. A song about being judged for how you look became, for some, a flag to wave.

[[The Business|9557fdd9-41a0-4029-84d9-cb3ae944ee8a]] covered it too.

eras.title: Grey keeps the name alive
eras.text: Back in the States, Grey started the Royal Americans, wrote novels and kept bringing Iron Cross back with new players. The early records finally came out together on CD.

years.h: Crucified For Our Sins collects the recordings
years.p: Lost and Found Records puts the Iron Cross material together.

years.h: Live for Now! gathers both EPs on one CD
years.p: GMM adds unreleased tracks. By now Iron Cross is a working band again.

years.h: Four Iron Cross songs, three from the Royal Americans
years.p: Two Piece and a Biscuit splits a record with Grey's rockabilly-ska-punk band. That year he also publishes a novel, Skinhead Army; Hated and Proud follows in 2009.
Skinflint releases the new EP. Medevev, who played on the 2009 lineup, dies the same year. Wikipedia gives no cause.
Asked by Vice about D.C.'s 1985 scene, he says he saw no revolution, only summer, and that most of its bands left him cold.
years.xp: "It may have been summer but I sure didn't see any revolution," Grey told Vice on October 29, 2012.

sources.title: Vice: We Interviewed Sab Grey From Iron Cross (2012)
